question: Under 22 TAC Section 535.2, a sponsoring broker must notify a sponsored sales agent in writing of:
choice_a: Nothing; sponsorship creates no notice obligations
choice_b: Only the agent's compensation split, with no mention of authorized activities
choice_c: The scope of the sales agent's authorized activities
choice_d: The agent's personal tax filing status
explanation: 22 TAC Section 535.2 requires a sponsoring broker to notify each sponsored sales agent in writing of the scope of activities the agent is authorized to perform; unless that scope is limited or revoked in writing, the broker remains responsible for the agent's authorized acts.
source_note: 22 TAC Section 535.2 (Broker Responsibility)

question: Under 22 TAC Section 535.2, a broker may delegate supervisory tasks to another license holder, but the broker:
choice_a: Is thereby fully released from any supervisory responsibility
choice_b: May delegate only to an unlicensed office administrator
choice_c: Must obtain TREC's advance written approval for every delegation
choice_d: May not relinquish overall responsibility for supervising all license holders sponsored by the broker
explanation: While 22 TAC Section 535.2 permits a broker to delegate day-to-day supervisory assistance to another qualified license holder, the sponsoring broker retains ultimate, non-delegable responsibility for overall supervision of everyone sponsored under the broker's license.
source_note: 22 TAC Section 535.2 (Broker Responsibility -- delegation of supervision)

question: Under 22 TAC Section 535.2, any license holder who leads, supervises, directs, or manages a real estate team must be:
choice_a: Delegated as a supervisor in writing
choice_b: Exempt from any TREC supervision rule as long as the team has a catchy brand name
choice_c: Automatically treated as the designated broker of the entire brokerage
choice_d: Prohibited from ever supervising other agents, regardless of experience
explanation: TREC's broker responsibility rule specifically addresses team structures, requiring that any license holder functioning as a team leader/supervisor be formally delegated that supervisory role in writing by the sponsoring broker, closing a gap where informal 'team leads' might otherwise escape accountability.
source_note: 22 TAC Section 535.2 (Broker Responsibility -- team supervision delegation)

question: Under TRELA Section 1101.558, a license holder representing a party in a proposed real estate transaction must disclose that representation:
choice_a: Only at closing, once all terms are finalized
choice_b: Orally or in writing at the time of the license holder's first contact with another party or the party's agent concerning the transaction
choice_c: Only if directly asked by the other party
choice_d: Never, since representation is presumed obvious to all parties
explanation: Section 1101.558 requires representation disclosure at the license holder's first contact with another party to the transaction or that party's agent, ensuring all participants understand who each licensee represents before substantive discussions occur.
source_note: Texas Occupations Code Section 1101.558 (Representation Disclosure)

question: Under TRELA Section 1101.559, a broker may lawfully represent both the buyer and seller in the same transaction by:
choice_a: Simply choosing to represent both without any special procedure or consent
choice_b: Delegating the entire transaction to an unlicensed assistant
choice_c: Acting as an intermediary, with written consent from both parties
choice_d: This is never permitted under any circumstance in Texas
explanation: Section 1101.559 establishes intermediary status as the sole lawful mechanism for one broker (or the broker's sponsored associates) to represent both parties in the same transaction, requiring written consent from both parties as a precondition.
source_note: Texas Occupations Code Section 1101.559 (Broker Acting as Intermediary)

question: Under TRELA Section 1101.560, a broker acting as an intermediary in a transaction may appoint:
choice_a: Only unlicensed staff to communicate with the parties
choice_b: The broker's spouse, regardless of licensure
choice_c: No one; the same individual license holder must personally handle both sides
choice_d: Separate associated license holders sponsored by the broker to work with and advise each party individually
explanation: Section 1101.560 permits an intermediary broker to appoint separate associated license holders to work with and provide opinions and advice to each party individually, which can approximate the experience of separate representation while the broker itself remains the neutral intermediary.
source_note: Texas Occupations Code Section 1101.560 (Associated License Holder Acting as Intermediary)

question: Under TRELA Section 1101.561, a broker acting as an intermediary must:
choice_a: Treat both parties fairly and impartially and may not act to advocate for one party's position to the other's detriment
choice_b: Openly advocate for whichever party pays the higher commission split
choice_c: Disclose one party's confidential negotiating position to the other party at will
choice_d: Represent only the seller once an offer is accepted
explanation: Section 1101.561 requires an intermediary to act fairly and impartially, without advocating for one party to the detriment of the other, and generally prohibits disclosing a party's confidential information (such as their willingness to pay more or accept less) to the other side without written authorization.
source_note: Texas Occupations Code Section 1101.561 (Duties of Intermediary)

question: A sponsored sales agent negotiates a transaction entirely outside the scope of activities the sponsoring broker authorized in writing. The broker's liability for that unauthorized conduct is generally:
choice_a: Identical in every respect regardless of whether the conduct was authorized
choice_b: Limited, since 22 TAC Section 535.2 ties broker responsibility to activities within the sales agent's authorized scope, absent other supervisory failures
choice_c: Nonexistent for the sales agent, who bears zero individual responsibility
choice_d: Automatically imputed to TREC itself
explanation: 22 TAC Section 535.2 conditions a broker's responsibility on the scope of authorized activities properly communicated in writing; conduct clearly outside that authorized scope may reduce (though not necessarily eliminate, depending on the facts and other supervisory obligations) the broker's exposure compared to conduct performed within the agent's authorized scope.
source_note: 22 TAC Section 535.2 (Broker Responsibility -- scope of authorized activities)

question: A designated broker for a licensed business entity is the individual who is:
choice_a: Merely a figurehead with no personal accountability
choice_b: Automatically the highest-producing agent in the office
choice_c: Personally responsible for the entity's broker responsibilities under 22 TAC Section 535.2
choice_d: Exempt from TREC's supervision rules because the license is held by the entity, not an individual
explanation: When a business entity holds the broker license, TREC rules designate a specific individual broker as personally responsible for the entity's broker responsibilities, ensuring an accountable natural person stands behind the entity's licensed activities.
source_note: 22 TAC Section 535.2 (Broker Responsibility -- designated broker); TREC guidance on designated brokers for business entities

question: A sales agent leaves one sponsoring broker to join another. Under TRELA, this change of sponsorship must be:
choice_a: Left unreported, since sponsorship changes are informal and require no notice to TREC
choice_b: Approved in advance by the prior sponsoring broker before the agent may join a new one
choice_c: Delayed for a mandatory six-month waiting period
choice_d: Properly reported to and processed by TREC so licensing records reflect the current sponsoring broker
explanation: A sales agent changing sponsoring brokers must ensure the change is properly reported and processed with TREC, since license records must accurately reflect who is currently responsible for supervising the agent's activities -- an agent practicing without an accurately recorded sponsorship risks operating as effectively unsponsored.
source_note: Texas Broker State Law Content Outline II.C.2 (Change of Sales Agent Sponsorship), Pearson VUE #094401

question: A sponsoring broker's use of an unlicensed assistant in the office is permissible only if the assistant:
choice_a: Performs only tasks that do not require a real estate license, such as clerical work, scheduling, or marketing preparation, under the broker's direction
choice_b: Personally negotiates purchase offers on the broker's behalf
choice_c: Independently determines listing prices for clients
choice_d: Signs contracts on behalf of licensed agents
explanation: Unlicensed assistants may perform ministerial, clerical, or administrative tasks that do not require a license, but they may not negotiate transactions, give advice about property value or contract terms, or otherwise perform activities that constitute licensed brokerage practice.
source_note: Texas Broker State Law Content Outline IV (Appropriate Use of Unlicensed Assistants), Pearson VUE #094401

question: Under TRELA's minimum services requirements, a broker representing a client under a limited-service listing agreement must still, at minimum:
choice_a: Provide absolutely no services at all, regardless of what the listing agreement states
choice_b: Provide certain baseline services defined by statute, such as accepting and presenting offers, even if other traditional services are excluded
choice_c: Guarantee the property will sell within 30 days
choice_d: Personally attend every showing of the property
explanation: TRELA's minimum services provisions ensure that even a limited-service or discount brokerage arrangement cannot waive certain baseline duties -- such as answering the client's questions and presenting all offers and counteroffers -- protecting consumers who choose reduced-service listing models.
source_note: Texas Broker State Law Content Outline IV (Duties to Client, including Minimum Services), Pearson VUE #094401

question: A broker who agrees to pay a sales agent's commission split under a written independent contractor agreement, but then attempts to unilaterally reduce that agreed split after a closing, has likely:
choice_a: Acted entirely within the broker's unrestricted discretion at all times
choice_b: Committed no violation, since brokers set all compensation unilaterally after the fact
choice_c: Violated the compensation terms of the broker-sales agent agreement, exposing the broker to a contract dispute (and potentially a TREC compensation-related complaint)
choice_d: Violated only tax law, with no real estate regulatory dimension
explanation: Compensation terms between a broker and sponsored sales agent are governed by their written agreement; unilaterally altering an agreed split after the agent has earned it under the contract's terms breaches that agreement and can also implicate TRELA's enforcement-of-compensation-agreement provisions if disputed.
source_note: Texas Broker State Law Content Outline IV (Enforcing Compensation Agreements, Broker-Sales Agent Relationships), Pearson VUE #094401

question: A broker acting as an intermediary who improperly discloses to the seller that the buyer would be willing to pay more than the buyer's current offer, without the buyer's written authorization, has violated:
choice_a: No duty, since intermediary brokers owe no confidentiality to either party
choice_b: Only a duty owed to the seller, since the seller benefited from the disclosure
choice_c: A duty that applies only in single-agency, not intermediary, transactions
choice_d: The confidentiality duty owed to the buyer under TRELA Section 1101.561
explanation: An intermediary broker under Section 1101.561 must maintain confidentiality of certain sensitive information (such as a party's true negotiating limits) unless the party has authorized disclosure in writing; improperly revealing that information to the other side breaches the intermediary's core statutory duty of impartiality and confidentiality.
source_note: Texas Occupations Code Section 1101.561 (Duties of Intermediary)

question: A broker's supervisory review of a sponsored agent's transaction files, advertising materials, and trust account activity, performed on a periodic basis, is a core requirement of:
choice_a: 22 TAC Section 535.2's broker responsibility standard
choice_b: Only voluntary best-practice guidance with no regulatory backing
choice_c: Federal antitrust law
choice_d: The Fair Housing Act
explanation: 22 TAC Section 535.2 grounds a sponsoring broker's affirmative supervisory obligation in ongoing, periodic review of sponsored agents' transaction documentation, marketing materials, and trust account handling -- not a one-time onboarding formality.
source_note: 22 TAC Section 535.2 (Broker Responsibility)

question: TREC's broker responsibility rule requires a sponsoring broker to respond to inquiries from sponsored agents within a reasonable time, sometimes summarized in practice as a:
choice_a: Requirement that applies only during regular business hours on weekdays, with no exceptions ever
choice_b: Prompt response requirement, ensuring supervision is meaningfully accessible rather than merely nominal
choice_c: One-year response window
choice_d: Rule that applies only to newly licensed agents in their first 90 days
explanation: 22 TAC Section 535.2's supervision framework contemplates that a sponsoring broker (or delegated supervisor) must be reasonably accessible and responsive to sponsored agents' questions and needs, since supervision that exists only on paper without meaningful accessibility fails to satisfy the broker's affirmative duty.
source_note: 22 TAC Section 535.2 (Broker Responsibility -- supervisory responsiveness)

question: A broker who is found to have failed to exercise adequate supervision over a sponsored sales agent's misconduct, even though the broker did not personally participate in the wrongdoing, may still face:
choice_a: No consequence at all, since only the individual agent who committed the misconduct can be disciplined
choice_b: Automatic criminal prosecution with no administrative process
choice_c: Independent TREC disciplinary action against the broker's own license for the supervisory failure itself
choice_d: Liability only if the broker personally profited from the misconduct
explanation: A broker's failure to exercise the affirmative supervisory duties required by 22 TAC Section 535.2 is itself an independent basis for TREC discipline against the broker, separate from whatever discipline the individual sales agent faces for the underlying misconduct.
source_note: 22 TAC Section 535.2 (Broker Responsibility); Texas Broker State Law Content Outline IV (Broker's Responsibility for Acts of Sales Agent), Pearson VUE #094401

question: A broker representing a seller receives two competing offers on the same day. Under the broker's duty to the seller-client, the broker must:
choice_a: Choose which offer to present based on which buyer's agent the broker personally prefers
choice_b: Present only the higher offer and discard the other without informing the seller
choice_c: Wait until both buyers agree on a single joint offer before presenting either
choice_d: Promptly present all offers received to the seller, unless the seller has given prior written instructions to withhold certain offers
explanation: A listing broker's fiduciary duty of disclosure and the broker's duties to the client require promptly presenting all offers received unless the seller has specifically instructed otherwise in writing (such as declining to see offers below a certain price), reinforcing transparency in a multiple-offer scenario.
source_note: Texas Broker State Law Content Outline IV (Duties to Client), Pearson VUE #094401

question: A sales agent working under an intermediary broker's appointment to represent the buyer's side of a transaction may:
choice_a: Provide opinions and advice during negotiations to the buyer they are appointed to work with, while the broker itself remains neutral as the intermediary
choice_b: Never provide any opinion or advice to either party under any circumstances
choice_c: Simultaneously act as the appointed representative for both the buyer and seller in the same transaction
choice_d: Ignore the buyer's instructions since the broker, not the sales agent, is the actual party in interest
explanation: Under Section 1101.560, an associated license holder appointed by an intermediary broker to work with one party may provide that party opinions and advice during negotiations, functioning much like a single-party representative, while the broker itself continues to occupy the neutral intermediary role overseeing the transaction.
source_note: Texas Occupations Code Section 1101.560 (Associated License Holder Acting as Intermediary)

question: A broker's decision to act as an intermediary in a transaction, rather than declining to represent both sides, must be based on:
choice_a: The broker's unilateral decision alone, with no need for party consent
choice_b: Written consent of both parties obtained in the manner required under TRELA Section 1101.559
choice_c: Verbal agreement only, with no writing required under any circumstance
choice_d: TREC's individual pre-approval of the specific transaction
explanation: Intermediary status is lawful only where both parties have given the written consent required under TRELA Section 1101.559 -- typically obtained through the buyer representation agreement, listing agreement, or a specific intermediary addendum -- not merely at the broker's discretion.
source_note: Texas Occupations Code Section 1101.559 (Broker Acting as Intermediary)

question: A broker's supervisory obligations under 22 TAC Section 535.2 extend to review of sponsored agents':
choice_a: Personal social media unrelated to any business use
choice_b: Private, non-business financial accounts
choice_c: Advertising materials, in addition to transaction documents and trust account handling
choice_d: Nothing beyond transaction paperwork; advertising is unregulated
explanation: 22 TAC Section 535.2's broker responsibility framework requires review extending to sponsored agents' advertising and marketing materials, not just transaction files, since improper advertising (such as omitting the sponsoring broker's name) is itself a compliance risk the broker must actively monitor.
source_note: 22 TAC Section 535.2 (Broker Responsibility -- review of advertising)

question: A sales agent sponsored by a broker signs a listing agreement in the agent's own individual name rather than the sponsoring broker's name. This practice is:
choice_a: Entirely proper and the preferred practice in Texas
choice_b: Irrelevant, since listing agreements need not identify any broker
choice_c: Required by TREC for every listing agreement
choice_d: Improper, since a sales agent's authority to enter brokerage agreements derives from and must reflect the sponsoring broker, who is the actual licensed broker of record
explanation: A sales agent acts only on behalf of and under the authority of the sponsoring broker; listing and other brokerage agreements should reflect the sponsoring broker as the actual contracting party, since the broker -- not the individual sales agent -- holds the underlying brokerage relationship and legal responsibility.
source_note: Texas Broker State Law Content Outline IV (Broker-Sales Agent Relationships), Pearson VUE #094401

question: A broker who terminates a sponsored sales agent's association must, among other obligations, ensure that:
choice_a: TREC's licensing records are properly updated to reflect the termination of sponsorship
choice_b: The agent is barred from ever obtaining sponsorship from any other broker
choice_c: The agent's license is physically destroyed by the broker
choice_d: Nothing; sponsorship terminations require no reporting or recordkeeping at all
explanation: When a sales agent's sponsorship ends, both the broker and the agent have obligations to ensure TREC's records are accurately and promptly updated, since a sales agent may not lawfully continue practicing real estate under a broker who no longer sponsors them.
source_note: Texas Broker State Law Content Outline II.C.2 (Change of Sales Agent Sponsorship), Pearson VUE #094401

question: In an intermediary transaction where no associated license holders are appointed, the broker acting alone as intermediary:
choice_a: Should freely advise whichever party asks first
choice_b: May not provide opinions or advice that favors either party's position over the other, consistent with the duty to remain neutral
choice_c: Automatically becomes the buyer's sole representative
choice_d: Is relieved of all disclosure obligations to both parties
explanation: When an intermediary broker acts without appointing separate associated license holders to each side, the broker's own neutrality is at its most constrained -- the broker must facilitate the transaction fairly and impartially without becoming an advocate or advisor favoring either party's negotiating position.
source_note: Texas Occupations Code Section 1101.561 (Duties of Intermediary)

question: A broker who sponsors sales agents across multiple office locations must ensure that supervisory coverage:
choice_a: Is required only at the broker's primary/main office, with satellite offices exempt
choice_b: Automatically transfers to whichever agent has been licensed the longest, with no formal delegation needed
choice_c: Is adequately maintained at each location, whether through the broker's own presence or a properly delegated supervisor
choice_d: Is entirely optional once a brokerage exceeds a certain size
explanation: 22 TAC Section 535.2's supervisory obligations apply across all of a broker's sponsored agents and locations; a broker operating multiple offices must ensure meaningful supervisory coverage everywhere, typically through properly delegated supervisors at each location rather than relying solely on the broker's own physical presence at one site.
source_note: 22 TAC Section 535.2 (Broker Responsibility); Texas Broker State Law Content Outline II.C.2 (Place of Business), Pearson VUE #094401

question: A broker's failure to provide the required written statutory notice at first substantive contact describing agency relationships and the broker's duties, including intermediary status, most directly violates:
choice_a: The Fair Housing Act
choice_b: RESPA's affiliated business disclosure rule
choice_c: The federal Truth in Lending Act
choice_d: TRELA Section 1101.558's representation disclosure requirement
explanation: Section 1101.558 specifically requires disclosure of representation -- describing how a broker can represent a party, including as an intermediary, and the broker's basic duties -- at the license holder's first contact, a distinctly Texas state-law requirement separate from federal disclosure statutes.
source_note: Texas Occupations Code Section 1101.558 (Representation Disclosure)

question: A broker's responsibility for a sales agent's acts under 22 TAC Section 535.2 can be limited if the broker:
choice_a: Properly limits or revokes the agent's scope of authorized activities in writing, and the agent's conduct falls outside that properly limited scope
choice_b: Simply claims after the fact not to have known about the agent's conduct, with no documentation
choice_c: Verbally tells the agent 'don't do that' with no written record
choice_d: Never; a broker is automatically responsible for every act of every sponsored agent regardless of any written limitation
explanation: 22 TAC Section 535.2 ties the scope of broker responsibility to the authorized activities the broker has communicated in writing; a broker who properly documents a limitation or revocation of an agent's authority, and whose conduct genuinely falls outside that documented scope, has a stronger basis to argue reduced responsibility -- underscoring why written, documented supervision matters so much in practice.
source_note: 22 TAC Section 535.2 (Broker Responsibility -- limiting or revoking scope in writing)

question: A broker considering whether to accept a dual role as intermediary in a transaction where the buyer and seller have conflicting negotiating goals should recognize that intermediary status:
choice_a: Gives the broker exactly the same advocacy latitude as representing only one party
choice_b: Is a lawful but constrained representation model requiring heightened neutrality, not a substitute for full single-party advocacy
choice_c: Is prohibited outright under all circumstances in Texas
choice_d: Requires no special disclosure or consent beyond a standard listing agreement
explanation: Intermediary practice is a lawful representation structure unique to Texas and a handful of other states, but it fundamentally constrains the broker's advocacy role compared to single-party representation, requiring brokers to carefully manage disclosures, appointments, and confidentiality to avoid inadvertently favoring one side.
source_note: Texas Occupations Code Sections 1101.559-1101.561 (Intermediary Practice)

question: A broker's sponsored sales agent asks whether they may independently hire and directly supervise their own unlicensed personal assistant without informing the sponsoring broker. The correct answer is that:
choice_a: The sales agent may do so entirely independently with zero broker involvement
choice_b: Unlicensed assistants are prohibited in Texas real estate offices altogether
choice_c: The sponsoring broker must still be aware of and ultimately responsible for the assistant's activities, since the broker cannot fully delegate away supervisory responsibility
choice_d: Only the assistant, not the sponsoring broker or the agent, bears any responsibility for the assistant's conduct
explanation: Because the sponsoring broker retains non-delegable overall responsibility for supervision under 22 TAC Section 535.2, even an agent's own personal unlicensed assistant's activities remain within the broker's supervisory concern, particularly regarding what tasks the assistant may lawfully perform without a license.
source_note: 22 TAC Section 535.2 (Broker Responsibility); Texas Broker State Law Content Outline IV (Appropriate Use of Unlicensed Assistants), Pearson VUE #094401
